cells.tense: Right now you stand where the next thing is already entering.
cells.act: finish the thing that has been waiting on its last step
cells.ask: Take the goal you're moving toward that only lacks its final move, and make that move. Then jot one unfinished line about what could follow it, and leave that line open.
cells.core:
You can face what's coming in without halting your forward motion. Most people notice the turning only once it's carried them somewhere; you can turn toward it mid-go and meet it while you're still under way. That changes what the moving is for. When the thing you've been heading for shows up, you neither grip it nor rush past into the next aim. It lands, you're in it, and the going holds.

When it lands, make the final move before any polish, then jot a single line for whatever comes after, and leave that line unfinished. A chapter that closes with its last page unsealed lets the next thing in. You'll know what that next thing wants when you read back what you set down for it.

cells.tense: You are bracing for a current that hasn't reached you yet.
cells.act: complete it without making it final
cells.ask: Choose the goal you're treating as done and finish only the piece genuinely ready this week. Name what the goal still holds open, then keep your hands off that part for now.
cells.core:
Where you move toward things, the bracing is toward arrivals that haven't come — carrying endings before the starts have done their work. The pull is steering and you're signing for it. The pattern repeats and its origin keeps living somewhere else. You can't outrun what's coming by pre-deciding what it will ask.

Take the goal you're already calling complete and finish just the piece that's actually ready. Then put a name on what it still leaves open and keep your hands off that part. Not all at once. A thing closed before it's finished doesn't free you; it moves the same cycle one step sideways and starts it over. Let one ending stay partial and stay there.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that closed behind you.
cells.act: close the cycle and leave the door open for the next
cells.ask: Find something already over that you haven't marked as over. Name it plainly, once, and start nothing in its place for a full week.
cells.core:
Moving toward things has gone quiet where you stand. Whatever you'd reach for feels as if it would only pull you back onto a turning you're trying to step off, so nothing gets picked up and nothing gets begun. What reads as peace is a position you're still holding after its moment passed. Meeting what arrives isn't far from you. It's one turn ahead of where you've parked.

Take something in your life that already finished and mark it finished, plainly, once, without ceremony. Don't install a replacement and don't hand its role to the next candidate. Let that stretch sit unclaimed for a week. The next thing comes in when the last one is acknowledged, not before. You don't need to choose it today; you only need to stop standing where the old one stood.

cells.tense: You are writing in a place you don't remember arriving at.
cells.act: choose this, not that, and mean it
cells.ask: Take one direction you're already moving in without having chosen it. Decide it's yours and not the other, mean it, and do one job only someone who chose it would do.
cells.core:
What happens downstream of you keeps taking you by surprise. Where you move toward goals, the motion is real and the aim belongs to something other than you — cycles turn and the outcomes read like the day's conditions. The pull runs. Nobody present recalls setting the bearing. You've been steering while calling it how things happen to go.

Pick one direction you're already travelling and claim it: this one, not that one. Nothing about the doing has to change. Say it belongs to you, mean it, then do one piece of work only someone who picked this path would do. Watch what comes of an outcome you signed for. That's the whole gap between being carried and going someplace on purpose.

attempts.check: The record gives no motive for what the person is doing, and no history for how the Drive seat emptied — the Too Little cell must locate them at the door without saying what happened there, and the Unacknowledged cell must name misattribution without naming what they tell themselves. A reader could reasonably say the Too Much cell assumes a life where conclusions actually land, and the ask will be useless if their real problem is that nothing in their life is finishable — but the act still teaches them which cycles are theirs to close. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line implying their Drive seat is broken rather than held, and it is cut from all four.
